concept.name: Ratio spread
concept.definition: A ratio spread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are sold than bought at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, long one call at a lower strike and short two calls at a higher strike. The extra short option(s) leave part of the position uncovered, giving the spread undefined or large risk beyond the short strikes.
concept.intuition: You finance a directional option purchase by selling two further-out options instead of one — cheap or free to enter, but the second short option is naked and can hurt badly in a big move.
concept.mechanics: Common ratios are 1x2 or 2x3. A 1x2 call ratio spread profits most if the underlying pins the short strike at expiration; beyond the upper breakeven the uncovered short call produces open-ended losses. Often established for a small debit, credit, or zero cost.
concept.formula: 1x2 call ratio payoff = max(S_T - K1, 0) - 2 x max(S_T - K2, 0) - net premium; upper breakeven = 2*K2 - K1 +/- net premium adjustment.
concept.failure_modes: The naked extra short leg converts a 'cheap' spread into an unlimited-risk position on the call side (or strike-sized risk on the put side); gap moves past the short strike realize losses that dwarf the initial outlay, and margin requirements reflect this.
concept.misconceptions: Zero-cost entry does not mean zero risk — the unpaid-for short option is exactly where the risk hides. Ratio spreads are not hedged spreads; they are spreads plus a naked option.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, buy one $100 call for $4.00 and sell two $105 calls for $2.00 each (zero cost). Max gain $5.00 at $105; above $110 the uncovered short call loses point-for-point without limit.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
